crisis? From the Colorado River to the world’s over-stressed river basins, solutions are stuck, waiting for funding and direction. By Mina Guli Thirst Foundation November 23, 2026 November 24, 2026 Share this article: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky By Mina Guli, CEO of the Thirst Foundation The American West’s water crisis is solvable. What’s missing is not interventions, or even money. It’s a $10 billion fund that can connect the two, using AI. It’s not the most obvious conclusion to arrive at, after running 2,000 miles down the entire length of the Colorado River in 92 grueling days. But as a water advocate who’s run more than 300 marathons in 32 countries, and someone who previously helped develop carbon initiatives at the World Bank, I see things differently. Yes, I witnessed the physical signs of a system in crisis this summer: depleted reservoirs, flash floods, and wildfires. But I also saw exactly how to save a river that’s a lifeline to the American West, supporting 40 million people and a $1.4 trillion annual economy. Despite the scale of the problem, interventions are going unfunded. I ran the Colorado River as part of “Keep the River Running,” a campaign supported by Danish water equipment maker Grundfos, the Walton Family Foundation, and Meta. It included summits in Denver, Las Vegas, Phoenix and Los Angeles to drive solutions to a crisis that threatens 16 million jobs, and critical hydropower, food supply, defense, and technology — including that of the AI industry, which has large hubs of hyperscalers in the river’s basin. It’s hard to understand that despite the scale of the problem, interventions are going unfunded. Yet I saw the evidence – methods of recharging aquifers with imitation beaver dams or reducing irrigation needs with solar panels are only adopted rarely. And at one point, a farmer showed me a new technology that reduced his water use by 30% and increased his yield by 17% – but said he couldn’t afford to buy it. It’s a common story among farmers, because the amounts they’re trying to access are too small to tap into big pools of capital.
